text:
**They Dont Work For You**

Why every VISA worker is cash in the pocket to everyone except the American Worker. 

Give me a break.

They told you this program exists because America cannot find talent. That is the official story. The unofficial story is just a simple spreadsheet.

If visa labor were only about rare genius, it would be a small, expensive, tightly policed tool. Instead it became a product line. The product is a warm body that is cheaper, quieter, harder to unionize, easier to move, less likely to sue, and useful as a billing unit on a government contract. 

Everyone in that chain makes money except the American who was supposed to report to the cafeteria for an important announcement, put their belongings in a box, and then go home and rot.

Start with the wage spread. Economic Policy Institute work on prevailing wage levels found that a majority of certified H-1B jobs were placed at the two lowest DOL wage tiers, below the local median for the occupation. 

A 2026 NBER paper estimated H-1B workers earn about 16 percent less than comparable natives in the same job, industry, and metro, which works out to more than $100,000 in payroll savings over a six-year term at typical tech salaries. HCL’s own internal materials, cited by EPI in a wage-theft case, showed the firm calculating large gaps versus its U.S. employees. Assumption on the floor: even a conservative 10 to 20 percent discount across hundreds of thousands of visa seats is not a rounding error.

It is a business model. 

It and it alone is enough to explain how millionaires became billionaires and how billion dollar companies became trillion dollar companies. 

Then the remittance pipe. The United States is the world’s largest source of outbound remittances, over $100 billion in recent official tallies. India is the world’s top receiver, on the order of $130 to $150 billion a year from all sources. Mexico takes roughly $60 to $68 billion, almost all of it from the United States, a few points of Mexican GDP. Formal U.S. outflows have been estimated around $93 billion, higher if you count informal channels. That cash is not a side effect.

It is USAID on steroids that American workers pay for while steadily losing buying power and prosperity.

It is a national interest for the sending countries and a political interest for the governments that do not want those workers coming home unemployed. Every threat results in millions more in lobbyist money coming back to entice our politicians to hold the line.

The lobbying. OpenSecrets has the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in the $70 million-plus range for a full year of federal lobbying (about $76 million in 2024, tens of millions already on the 2026 clock). Labor, workplace rules, and immigration sit inside that spend along with everything else the Chamber wants. ITServe Alliance is smaller on the official LDA line, on the order of $180,000 a year in recent filings, plus a PAC that writes four-figure and five-figure checks to both parties. Do not confuse the filing with the operation. ITServe is a 2,000-firm trade group with Hill days that have claimed meetings with 85, then 145, then nearly 180 offices of BOTH PARTIES. 

Ever hear how these work? Typically, and you can look this up, the meeting starts with an envelope of money presented to the politician. It's legal. 

Its own materials describe the method in three words: educate, lobby, and litigate. That is how itinerary rules and wage hikes get sued into the dirt.

Now the parts that do not show up as a line item.

Union risk. A worker whose status is tied to one employer is a worse organizing target than a citizen who can walk. Assumption: firms price that. They do not need a memo that says “import a non-union shop.” They need a workforce that will not vote in a bargaining unit.

Lawsuit risk. FLSA and HR complaints from visa holders exist, and some win. The pattern still favors the sponsor. Status, debt, benching, and the next petition are leverage. A citizen can file and stay in the labor market. A visa holder can file and lose the country. Assumption: that discount is real even when it is not itemized.

Contract risk. Public-sector IT gets layered through vendors. The agency pays a loaded rate. The body on the badge may be a visa worker several subcontractors down. Fewer local employees means fewer local whistleblowers who know the building, the code, and the billing. Assumption: that is why integrators like the model and why taxpayers rarely see the stack.

Add the university seat, the OPT year, the H-4 household, the staffing margin, the offshore cousin doing the tickets, and the politician who gets the fly-in and the check. You do not need a cartoon villain. You need aligned incentives.

That is why the program is so hard to kill. Americans are the residual claimant. Employers keep the wage gap. Staffing firms keep the spread. Universities keep tuition. Foreign treasuries keep remittances. Lobby shops keep retainers. Contractors keep the award. Politicians keep the donor. The only group whose profit depends on ending it is the group that does not have a PAC.

Give me a break. This was never a mystery of talent. It is a map of who gets paid when the American stays home.

They Dont Work For You.

If you have seen the wage gap, the vendor stack, or the Hill talking points in your own shop, put the pattern in the comments. Like share and bookmark this. Follow for more.

Sources and assumptions

OpenSecrets. U.S. Chamber of Commerce federal lobbying about $76.4 million in 2024; 2026 midyear already in the high tens of millions.

OpenSecrets / OpenLobby / FEC. ITServe Alliance lobbying about $180,000 a year in recent cycles. ITServe PAC candidate contributions about $21,000 in 2023-24, split both parties. ITServe Alliance FY2024 revenue about $8 million per nonprofit filings.

ITServe public materials. Capitol Hill Days and “educate, lobby, and litigate.”

World Bank / IOM / IDB / Niskanen. India remittance inflows roughly $130 to $151 billion depending on year and series. Mexico roughly $62 to $68 billion, mostly from the U.S. U.S. as top outbound source, formal estimates around $93 to $100-plus billion.

Economic Policy Institute (Costa and Hira). Majority of H-1B certifications at the two lowest prevailing wage levels, below local median.

NBER working paper w34793 (2026). About 16 percent average pay gap versus comparable natives; implied six-year payroll savings over $100,000 at typical salaries.

EPI on HCL internal wage comparisons. Firm-calculated gaps versus U.S. staff, alleged actual-wage violations.

Assumptions labeled above: union-avoidance value, lower FLSA/HR exposure, fewer whistleblowers on stacked public contracts, and scaling a 10 to 20 percent wage discount across the visa stock. Those are inferences from structure and testimony, not a single audited national total.

Section 16 of the DPDP Act lets the Government bar transfers of personal data to named countries. No country has been named, so personal data may leave India freely today.

The direction is the reverse of GDPR, which blocks transfers until a destination is approved. A section 16 notification needs no consultation and carries no transition period, and sectoral rules such as the RBI's payment data directive continue to apply regardless.

#DPDP #dataprotection #surispeaks

The largest penalty in the DPDP Act attaches to the safeguard, not the leak. Section 8(5) requires reasonable security safeguards, and the Schedule sets the penalty for failing that duty at up to 250 crore rupees.

The Board can impose it without a single record going missing, because the breach of duty is the missing safeguard itself. The duty binds from 13 May 2027.

The DPDP Act defines a child as anyone under eighteen. Mishandling children's data carries a penalty of up to 200 crore rupees, the same tier as failing to notify a breach.

Consent must come from a parent and be verifiable under Rule 10, and section 9(3) bans tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children. All of it takes effect on 13 May 2027.

text:
India clearing administrative satcom spectrum at 5% AGR (4% in notified remote/border pockets) is being framed as an open runway for Starlink.

​The regulatory fine print and unit economics tell a very different story.

​What most headlines missed, and how this truly reshapes Indian telecom:
​
1. The True Cost: A 13% Total Regulatory Toll
The 5% spectrum charge isn’t the only levy. Satcom operators must still pay the standard 8% annual telecom license fee.
A total 13% AGR levy—coupled with zero terminal subsidies (the DoT rejected TRAI’s proposal to subsidize dishes via the Digital Bharat Nidhi fund)—rules out aggressive retail price dumping.
​
2. The Rejection of the Urban Disincentive
TRAI recommended a ₹500/year surcharge per urban subscriber to force operators deep into the hinterland.
The DoT scrapped it. Why? Policing dynamic satellite spot beams across fluid administrative boundaries is technically unworkable.
This greenlights high-paying, remote enterprise pockets (mining belts, maritime vessels, defense corridors, infrastructure builds, luxury eco-resorts) to cross-subsidize expensive user terminals.
​
3. Does This Threaten Jio & Airtel's Retail Broadband? No.
​ARPU Realities: Indian fibre/5G FWA already sits at ₹500–₹1,000/month. Starlink-class terminals are ₹25,000–₹40,000. That is not a home-broadband fight in tier-1 to tier-3 towns.
​Physics & Capacity: LEO is a coverage and backhaul layer. It does not replace mass retail broadband over a dense metro.

​4. The Real Competitive Playbook
​▪️$BHARTIARTL - Built an early enterprise moat. Backed by Eutelsat OneWeb, Airtel already has licensed Indian ground stations and B2B corporate contracts ready to flip the switch.
​▪️Reliance Jio: Jio Space (partnered with SES via MEO/GEO) isn't chasing rooftop dishes; they will use satcom to backhaul remote 4G/5G cell towers where laying terrestrial fiber is economically unviable.

​Domestic Satellite Ecosystem Plays:
​▪️$NELCO (Tata Group) & Hughes India: Strong legacy enterprise and maritime satcom providers that now face direct LEO competition.
​▪️$AVANTEL & $DATAPATTNS - Base station gateways, defense RF electronics, and satellite transceivers see structural domestic demand as gateway infrastructure expands.
​
Satcom in India isn't an urban consumer price war; it’s a high-margin enterprise, defense, and cellular backhaul play.

​(Educational only. Not investment advice.)

The BJP's record on press freedom deserves scrutiny. But that cannot give Congress, AAP or any other ruling party a free pass.

The examples in this video raise serious questions — and several are independently reported.

In Kerala, journalist Aparna Kurup was booked after a TV debate in which she criticised controversial remarks by cleric Kanthapuram A.P. Aboobacker Musliyar about women. Police invoked provisions concerning provocation, religious feelings and communal enmity. Kurup had herself earlier complained of threats following the debate. 

In Karnataka, journalist G. Mahantesh of The File reported on court proceedings concerning a trust linked to the Kharge family. He subsequently alleged abusive calls and death threats demanding that his reports be removed. Police have registered an FIR against an unidentified person and are investigating. 

In Telangana, two women journalists were arrested in 2025 over a video critical of Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy, following a complaint by a Congress worker. 

And in Punjab, an investigation by The Reporters' Collective documented at least 48 copyright claims against posts and videos by journalists critical of the AAP government, with several Facebook pages subsequently removed. 

These cases are not identical. Some involve police cases, some alleged threats, and some copyright takedowns. They should not be casually presented as proof of one coordinated policy.

But they establish something more important:

Press freedom must be tested by what governments tolerate when journalists investigate THEM.

If the BJP suppresses dissent — condemn it.

If Congress does it — condemn it.

If AAP does it — condemn it.

The standard cannot change with the colour of the government.

A free press is not a favour granted by the party in power.

It is a democratic right that exists precisely to question power.

Under the Constitution of India, executive authority is neither absolute nor immune from scrutiny. Freedom of expression is not a privilege granted at the whim of the state,pĺit is a fundamental right forged to ensure those who govern remain answerable to those they govern.
When leaders dodge critical questions, silence scrutiny, or walk away from the microphone, it is not merely political evasion. It is an act of defiance against democratic accountability. It signals a dangerous premise, that power owes no explanation to the people.
Evasion is not strength,it is cowardice. A democracy rots when public servants/Ministers  treat public questioning as an inconvenience. Those who demand the authority to govern must have the courage to answer.

@TeamYouTube this situation has gone way beyond a normal enforcement issue. On July 28, my channel started receiving an unusual wave of privacy complaints. Within roughly 3 days, 40+ complaints were filed against 41 completely unrelated videos, and 31 videos were removed. I appealed multiple removals and repeatedly contacted YouTube Support and Legal, but I never received a clear, case-specific explanation of the alleged privacy violations.

Then on August 14, the entire channel was terminated for Impersonation. I appealed and was rejected. When I contacted Creator Support, I was first told the termination was for Spam, despite the termination notice clearly stating Impersonation. The case was escalated, and I was then told the internal review confirmed Impersonation. I repeatedly asked a simple question: Who or what did I supposedly impersonate, and what exactly on the channel violated the policy? No specific answer was provided.

I submitted another official appeal through Google Form. It was confirmed as received and sent for specialized review, but that appeal has now also been rejected for Impersonation.

So after multiple reviews, I still haven't been told what specific person, channel, branding, video, or conduct supposedly constituted impersonation. I have never intentionally impersonated anyone or claimed to represent another creator or entity.

The matter is now pending before GAC in India and has also been brought to @SFLCin.

I am not asking for special treatment. I am asking for a fair, evidence-based review and a clear explanation of what actually happened. Please escalate this properly and reconsider the termination. @YouTube @UpdatesFromYT @YouTubeCreators @YouTubeIndia

Ray-Ban Meta glasses struck again. A woman walking home alone was secretly recorded by a man who approached her, then posted the footage on Instagram alongside similar clips of him doing this to other women, as part of "pickup" content.

She's filed a police complaint for stalking and voyeurism. IFF is assisting her with a legal notice to the creator, Instagram, and Meta, the second such notice against Meta in India.

This isn't a one off. It's a design problem.
Read more about it: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

A woman was followed, stopped on a dark street, secretly recorded through Ray-Ban Meta glasses and turned into an Instagram “pickup” reel that reached over 23 lakh views. Now, our legal notice seeks accountability from both him and Meta. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

The legal notice therefore puts Meta on notice not merely as the platform hosting the video, but as the designer, developer, manufacturer, marketer and seller of the glasses. It alleges negligence and product liability, arguing that Meta knew about the pattern of misuse but continued selling the device without an effective way for non-users or people being recorded to report that misuse. (9/10)

The notice seeks removal of every copy, preservation and disclosure of evidence, suspension of monetisation, an account of profits, an apology, and ₹2.05 crore in compensatory and exemplary damages. This case raises a larger question: when a company makes a camera that can be worn like ordinary glasses, who protects the person being recorded? Privacy cannot depend on whether the person being filmed has an Instagram account. (10/10)

The Supreme Court has closed India's Got Latent cases, but the question of an “Influencer Code” is not entirely over. On 14 August 2026, the Court quashed all FIRs arising from the episode and left the “larger issues” of regulating online speech for “another appropriate case”. Here is what that means. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/hecp2rl9W4

That qualifier matters. Executive action restricting speech must have a legal basis consistent with Article 19. The Court has previously held that executive instructions cannot independently impose restrictions on fundamental rights. The signed order also contains no finding that the content in question was obscene, nor does it establish a new standard for online speech. (6/7)

For now, there are no guidelines and no pending judicial direction requiring them. But MIB can still attempt regulatory changes, including through amendments to the IT Rules. If it does, IFF will insist on the public consultation promised to the Supreme Court, compliance with the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy and meaningful participation by affected creators and users. (7/7)

NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. On 8 September, IFF wrote back seeking a standstill and answers. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2grOxR1bMy

The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)

NIXI has now also said that six other .in domains containing “Sansad”, along with other domains containing “Sansad”, “Parliament” or cognate expressions, will be examined. On 8 September, we asked NIXI for a 48-hour standstill on de-registration, deletion, transfer or reallocation of chalosansad dot in, confirmation of Aadhaar deletion, and disclosure of the correspondence it says raised concerns about publication. If no standstill is given, the registrant will approach the court. (7/7)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

NIXI has also given the registrant seven days to produce Central Government permission. Yet its reply identifies no ministry, officer, form, fee, procedure or timeline through which such permission can actually be obtained. We have therefore asked NIXI to explain the legal basis for this demand, and to provide the legal opinion dated 29 August on which its new position relies. (5/7)

quotedTweet.text:
On September 10th, 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, a vague law that was being used to arrest people for simply expressing dissent online.

11 years later, Maharashtra wants to bring it back in a new form, by amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "online criminal defamation." But defamation is already covered under Section 356 of the BNS, and civil remedies already exist.

So why does the police need this new power? Recent FIRs against citizens and influencers for calling out potholes and infrastructure failures may hold the answer. We've fought this battle before. We don't need a new 66A with a new number.

text:
A 2:01-minute reel documenting villagers’ concerns over the proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India for 111 days. On 10 September 2026, it quietly came back online. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/TVxhdw9ZA1

The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. Section 79(3)(b), meanwhile, was read down to require a court order or government notification. A system that blocks first and explains nothing is difficult to reconcile with those safeguards. (9/10)

The reel is back, and we welcome that. But the questions remain unanswered, Who ordered the blocking? Why did the order name an unrelated person? Was a periodic review conducted? Why was the reel restored? IFF will continue seeking these answers from Andhra Pradesh authorities. Journalists should not need months of litigation to learn why their public-interest reporting was censored. (10/10)
